It may also be agreed, for the event of survival, that one of the spouses shall have, in addition to his or her half, the usufruct of the share of the predeceased. In that case, he or she shall contribute to the debts, as to the usufruct, according to the rules of Articles 714 and following of this code.  
The provisions of Article 1731 are applicable to these clauses when the community is dissolved during the lifetime of both spouses.

###### Article 1736

The stipulation of unequal shares and the clause of full attribution are not deemed to constitute donations, either as to substance or as to form, but simply marriage contracts and between partners. Unless otherwise stipulated, they do not prevent the heirs of the predeceased spouse from recovering the contributions and capital that fell into the community from their predecessor.

###### Sous-section 6 : De la communauté universelle

The spouses may establish by their marriage contract a universal community of their property both movable and immovable, present and future. However, unless otherwise stipulated, the property that Article 1651 declares to be separate by its nature does not fall into this community.  

The universal community definitively bears all the debts of the spouses, present and future.

##### Section III

Dispositions communes aux deux premières sections du chapitre II Article 1738
The advantages that either spouse may derive from the clauses of a conventional community, as well as those that may result from the merger of movable property or debts, are not regarded as constituting donations.  

Nevertheless, in the event that there are children who are not issue of both spouses, any agreement that would have the consequence of giving to one of the spouses beyond the portion regulated by Article 1228, under the title Of Inter Vivos Donations and Wills, shall be without effect for the entire excess; but the simple benefits resulting from common work and savings made from the respective incomes, although unequal, of the two spouses, are not considered as an advantage made to the prejudice of children of another marriage.

#### Chapitre III : Du régime de séparation de biens Article 1739

When the spouses have stipulated in their marriage contract that they would be separate as to property, each of them retains the administration, enjoyment and free disposition of his or her personal property.  

Each of them remains solely liable for debts arising in his or her person before or during the marriage, except in the case of Article 228.

###### Article 1740

Spouses contribute to the expenses of the marriage according to the agreements contained in their marriage contract; and, if there are none in this regard, in the proportion determined in Article 222.

###### Article 1741

Both with regard to his or her spouse and to third parties, a spouse may prove by all means that he or she has exclusive ownership of property.  
The presumptions of ownership stated in the marriage contract have effect with regard to third parties as well as in relations between spouses, unless otherwise agreed. Proof to the contrary shall be permitted, and it shall be made by all means capable of establishing that the property does not belong to the spouse designated by the presumption, or even, if it belongs to him or her, that he or she acquired it by a liberality from the other spouse.  

Property over which neither spouse can establish exclusive ownership is deemed to belong to them jointly, to each for one half.

###### Article 1742

If, during the marriage, one of the spouses entrusts the other with the administration of his or her personal property, the rules of mandate are applicable. The spouse acting as mandatary is, however, dispensed from accounting for the fruits, when the power of attorney does not expressly require it.  

When one of the spouses takes over the management of the property of the other, with the latter's knowledge, and nevertheless without opposition on his or her part, he or she is deemed to have received a tacit mandate, covering acts of administration and management, but not acts of disposition.  

That spouse is liable for his or her management to the other as a mandatary. He or she is, however, accountable only for existing fruits; for those which he or she has neglected to collect or fraudulently consumed, he or she may be pursued only within the limit of the last five years.  

If it is in defiance of a recorded opposition that one of the spouses has interfered in the management of the property of the other, he or she is liable for all the consequences of his or her interference, and accountable without limitation for all the fruits which he or she has collected, neglected to collect or consumed.

###### Article 1744

A spouse is not liable for the failure to invest or reinvest the property of the other, unless he or she has interfered in the operations of alienation or collection, or unless it is proved that the monies were received by him or her, or were used for his or her benefit.

###### Article 1745

After the dissolution of the marriage by the death of one of the spouses, the partition of undivided property between spouses separated as to property, with respect to all matters concerning its forms, the maintenance of joint ownership and preferential attribution, the sale by auction of property, the effects of partition, the warranty and the balancing payments, is subject to all the rules which are established in the Title on Successions for partitions between co-heirs.  
The same rules apply after divorce or legal separation. However, preferential attribution is never automatic. It may always be decided that the whole of any balancing payment due shall be payable in cash.

###### Article 1746

The rules of Article 1707 are applicable to claims that one of the spouses may have to exercise against the other.

#### Chapitre IV : Du régime de participation aux acquêts Article 1747

When the spouses have declared that they are marrying under the regime of participation in acquisitions, each of them retains the administration, enjoyment and free disposal of his or her personal property, without distinguishing between those which belonged to him or her on the day of the marriage or came to him or her since by succession or liberality and those which he or she acquired during the marriage for valuable consideration. During the duration of the marriage, this regime functions as if the spouses were married under the regime of separation of property. Upon dissolution of the regime, each of the spouses has the right to participate for one half in value in the net acquisitions recorded in the patrimony of the other, and measured by the double valuation of the original patrimony and the final patrimony.  
The right to participate in acquisitions is not transferable as long as the matrimonial regime is not dissolved. If the dissolution occurs by the death of a spouse, his or her heirs have, over the net acquisitions made by the other, the same rights as their predecessor.

###### Article 1748

The original patrimony comprises the property which belonged to the spouse on the day of the marriage and that which he or she has acquired since by succession or liberality, as well as all property which, in the regime of legal community, forms separate property by nature without giving rise to compensation. No account is taken of the fruits of such property, nor of such property which would have had the character of fruits or which the spouse has disposed of by inter vivos donation during the marriage.  

The composition of the original patrimony is proved by a descriptive statement, even under private signature, established in the presence of the other spouse and signed by him or her. In the absence of a descriptive statement or if it is incomplete, proof of the composition of the original patrimony may be adduced only by the means of Article 1649.

###### Article 1749

Original property is valued according to its condition on the day of the marriage or of the acquisition, and according to its value on the day when the matrimonial regime is liquidated. If it has been alienated, its value on the day of the alienation is retained. If new property has been subrogated to the alienated property, the value of such new property is taken into consideration.  
From the original assets are deducted the debts with which it was encumbered, revalued, if necessary, according to the rules of Article 1697. If the liabilities exceed the assets, this excess is notionally added to the final patrimony.

###### Article 1750

The final patrimony comprises all property which belongs to the spouse on the day when the matrimonial regime is dissolved, including, where applicable, that which he or she would have disposed of by reason of death and without excluding the sums of which he or she may be a creditor towards his or her spouse. If there is divorce, legal separation or early liquidation of acquisitions, the matrimonial regime is deemed dissolved on the day of the application.  
The composition of the final patrimony is proved by a descriptive statement, even under private signature, which the spouse or his or her heirs must establish in the presence of the other spouse or his or her heirs or they being duly summoned. This statement must be drawn up within nine months of the dissolution of the matrimonial regime, subject to extension by the President of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance ruling in summary proceedings.  

Proof that the final patrimony would have comprised other property may be adduced by all means, even by testimony and presumptions.  

Each of the spouses may, as regards the property of the other, require the affixing of seals and the inventory according to the rules provided in the code of civil procedure.

###### Article 1751

To existing property are notionally added property which does not appear in the original patrimony and which the spouse has disposed of by inter vivos donation without the consent of his or her spouse, as well as that which he or she would have alienated fraudulently. Alienation subject to a life annuity or for a lump sum is presumed made in fraud of the rights of the spouse, if the latter has not consented to it.

###### Article 1752

Existing property is valued according to its condition at the time of the dissolution of the matrimonial regime and according to its value on the day of the liquidation thereof. Property which has been alienated by inter vivos donations, or in fraud of the rights of the spouse, is valued according to its condition on the day of the alienation and the value which it would have had, if it had been retained, on the day of liquidation.  
From the assets thus reconstituted, all debts which have not yet been paid are deducted, including sums which might be owed to the spouse. The value, on the day of the alienation, of improvements which had been made during the marriage to original property given by a spouse without the consent of his or her spouse before the dissolution of the matrimonial regime must be added to the final patrimony.

###### Article 1753

If the final patrimony of a spouse is less than his or her original patrimony, the deficit is borne entirely by that spouse. If it is greater, the increase represents the net acquests and gives rise to participation.  

If there are net acquests on both sides, they must first be offset. Only the excess is shared: the spouse whose gain was the lesser is a creditor of his or her spouse for half of that excess.  

To the participation claim are added, to subject them to the same settlement, the sums for which the spouse may otherwise be a creditor towards his or her spouse, for values provided during the marriage and other indemnities, after deducting, if applicable, what he or she may owe to the other.

###### Article 1754

The participation claim gives rise to payment in money. If the debtor spouse encounters serious difficulties in discharging it entirely upon closure of the liquidation, the judges may grant him or her delays not exceeding five years, subject to providing security and paying interest. The amount of such interest is determined by mutual agreement and, failing that, the legal interest rate shall apply.  
The participation claim may however give rise to settlement in kind, either with the consent of both spouses, or pursuant to a decision of the judge, if the debtor spouse establishes serious difficulties preventing him or her from discharging it in money.  
The settlement in kind provided for in the preceding paragraph is considered a partition operation when the assets allocated were not included in the original patrimony or when the spouse receiving the allocation succeeds to the other.  

The liquidation is not enforceable against the creditors of the spouses: they retain the right to seize the assets allocated to the spouse of their debtor.

###### Article 1755

The creditor spouse pursues recovery of his or her participation claim first against existing assets and, subsidiarily, beginning with the most recent alienations, against the assets mentioned in Article 1751 that had been alienated by inter vivos donation or in fraud of the rights of the spouse.

###### Article 1756

Upon dissolution of the matrimonial regime, if the parties do not agree to proceed with liquidation by agreement, one of them may request the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance to proceed therewith.  
Applicable to this request, as appropriate, are the rules prescribed for arriving at judicial partition of successions and communities.  

The parties are required to communicate to each other reciprocally, and to communicate to the experts appointed by the judge, all information and documents useful for the liquidation. The action for liquidation is prescribed after three years from the dissolution of the matrimonial regime. Actions brought against third parties pursuant to Article 920, paragraph 4, are prescribed after two years from the closure of the liquidation.

###### Article 1757

If the application of the valuation rules provided for by Articles 1749 and 1752 should lead to a result manifestly contrary to equity, which the judge must specially justify, the court may derogate therefrom at the request of one of the spouses.

###### Article 1758

If the disorder of the affairs of a spouse, his or her poor administration or his or her misconduct, give rise to fear that the continuation of the matrimonial regime may compromise the interests of the other spouse, the latter may request early liquidation of his or her participation claim.  
The rules of separation of property are applicable to this request. When the request is granted, the spouses are placed under the regime of Articles 1739 to 1744.

###### Article 1759

By stipulating participation in acquests, the spouses may adopt any clauses not contrary to Articles 1633, 1635 and 1636. They may in particular agree to a clause of unequal partition, or stipulate that the survivor of them or one of them if he or she survives, shall be entitled to all of the net acquests made by the other. It may also be agreed between the spouses that the one of them who, upon liquidation of the regime, will have a participation claim against the other, may require dation in payment of certain assets of his or her spouse, if he or she establishes that he or she has an essential interest in having them allocated to him or her.

### Title VII: On Sale

Chapter I. On the Nature and Form of Sale Article 1760
Sale is a contract by which one party undertakes to deliver a thing, and the other to pay for it. It may be made by authentic act, executed under private signature, or verbally.

###### Article 1761

The sale is perfect between the parties, and ownership is acquired by right by the buyer with respect to the seller, as soon as the parties have agreed on the thing and on its price, even if the thing has not yet been delivered nor the price paid.

###### Article 1762

The sale may be made purely and simply, or subject to a condition, which may be suspensive or resolutory.  
It may also have as its object two or more alternative things.  

In all these cases, its effect is governed by the general principles provided for by this code and which govern the contract.

###### Article 1763

When goods are not sold in bulk, but by weight, count or measure, the sale is not perfect: the things sold remain at the risk of the seller until they are weighed, counted or measured; but, in case of non-performance of his undertaking by the seller, the buyer may demand delivery of the thing or damages, if applicable.  
On the other hand, if the goods have been sold in bulk, the sale is perfect, regardless of the fact that the goods have not yet been weighed, counted or measured.

###### Article 1764

In case of sale on trial, as for wine, oil, and other things that one is in the habit of tasting before making the purchase, there is no sale until the buyer has tasted and approved them.  
Such a sale is always presumed made subject to a suspensive condition.

###### Article 1765

The promise of sale is equivalent to sale, as soon as there is reciprocal consent of both parties on the thing and on the price.  
When a unilateral promise to sell land already subdivided or to be subdivided is signed, the exercise of the option necessarily results from payment of part of the price by the beneficiary of the promise, whatever

the name given by the parties to that payment, provided that he has taken possession of the immovable property that is the subject of the act.  

The date of the agreement, even if regularized subsequently, shall be that of payment of the first installment.

###### Article 1766

Any unilateral undertaking entered into with a view to acquiring immovable property or an immovable right for which a payment is required or received from the person undertaking, whatever its cause and form, is null and void.

###### Article 1767

If it is not evidenced by an authentic instrument or by a private instrument registered within ten days from the date of its acceptance by the beneficiary, any unilateral promise to sell relating to immovable property, an immovable right, a business, a right to a lease covering all or part of an immovable, or to shares in companies whose shares or units confer upon their holders the right to enjoyment of immovables or fractions of immovables and to those of companies which have, in fact, as their sole purpose either the construction or acquisition of immovables or groups of immovables with a view to their division into fractions intended to be allocated to the members in ownership or enjoyment, or the management of such immovables or groups of immovables thus divided, or the lease on behalf of one or more members of the company of all or part of the immovables or fractions of immovables belonging to each of these members, shall be null and void.  
The same applies to any assignment relating to said promises which has not been the subject of an authentic instrument or a private instrument registered within ten days of its date.

###### Article 1768

If the promise to sell has been made with a deposit, each of the contracting parties has the possibility of withdrawing from the contract:
The one who gave it, by forfeiting the sum represented by the deposit paid, And the one who received the deposit, by returning double the sum received.  
Unless otherwise stipulated, for any contract of sale or provision of services concluded between a professional and a consumer, sums paid in advance are deposits.

###### Article 1769

The price of the sale must be determined and designated by the parties.

###### Article 1770

The parties to the contract may, however, designate a third party to estimate the price of the sale; if the third party does not wish or cannot make the estimate, there is no sale.  
If the expert has not been designated due to the silence or conduct of one of the parties to the contract, its non-performance is resolved in damages.  
The price fixed by the expert may only be challenged in the event of a gross error on his part in its determination.

###### Article 1771

Unless otherwise stipulated, the costs of instruments and other accessories to the sale are borne by the purchaser.

#### Chapitre II. Qui peut acheter ou vendre Article 1772

All those whom the law does not prohibit may buy or sell.

###### Article 1773

The contract of sale may not take place between spouses except in the following three cases:
1° Where one of the two spouses transfers property to the other, judicially separated from him, in payment of his rights;  
2° Where the transfer that the husband makes to his wife, even if not separated, has a legitimate cause, such as the reinvestment of her alienated immovables, or of monies belonging to her, if such immovables or monies do not fall into community property;  
3° Where the wife transfers property to her husband in payment of a sum which she would have promised him as a dowry, and when there is exclusion of community property;  
subject, in these three cases, to the rights of the heirs of the contracting parties, if there is an indirect advantage.

###### Article 1774

May not become purchasers at auction, under penalty of nullity, either by themselves or through intermediaries:	guardians, of the property of those of whom they have guardianship;	mandataries, of the property which they are charged with selling;	administrators, of those of the communes or public establishments entrusted to their care;	public officers, of national property the sales of which are made through their ministry.	fiduciaries, of property or rights composing the fiduciary patrimony.

###### Article 1775

It is prohibited for persons invested with judicial functions, such as judges, their substitutes, magistrates of the public prosecution, court clerks, bailiffs, notaries, lawyers or any other person authorized to represent others in court, to acquire rights or actions liable to be contested before the court within whose jurisdiction they exercise their functions.

#### Chapitre III. Des choses qui peuvent être vendues Article 1776

Except where the law provides otherwise, everything that is in commerce may be sold.

###### Article 1777

The following are null and void:
1° The sale of another person's property. Such a sale may give rise to damages when the purchaser was unaware that the property belonged to another;  
2° The succession of a living person, even with his consent;  
3° The sale of a thing which did not exist or no longer existed at the time of the sale. The purchaser may then, at his option, abandon the sale or request the preserved part of the thing with a reduction in price in a proportion analogous to that of the loss incurred.

#### Chapitre IV. De la vente d'immeubles à construire Article 1778

The sale of immovables to be constructed is that by which the seller undertakes to erect an immovable within a period determined by the contract.  
It may be concluded on a fixed term basis or in a future state of completion.

###### Article 1779

The sale on a fixed term is the contract by which the seller undertakes to deliver the immovable upon its completion, the purchaser undertakes to take delivery of it and to pay the price on the date of delivery. The transfer of

ownership takes place by operation of law upon the recording by authentic instrument of the completion of the immovable; it produces its effects retroactively to the day of the sale.

###### Article 1780

The sale in a future state of completion is the contract by which the seller immediately transfers to the purchaser his rights over the land as well as the ownership of existing constructions. Future works become the property of the purchaser as and when they are executed; the purchaser is required to pay the price as the works progress.  
The seller retains the powers of project owner until acceptance of the works.

###### Article 1781

The assignment by the purchaser of the rights which he holds from a sale of immovable to be constructed substitutes by operation of law the assignee in the obligations of the purchaser towards the seller.  
If the sale has been accompanied by a mandate, it continues between the seller and the assignee.  
These provisions apply to any transfer inter vivos, voluntary or forced, or upon death.

#### Chapitre V. Des obligations du vendeur

##### Section I : Dispositions générales Article 1782

The seller is required to explain clearly what he undertakes to do. Any obscure or ambiguous clause is interpreted against the seller.  
In contracts proposed by professionals to consumers, clauses must be presented and drafted in a clear and comprehensible manner. In case of doubt, they are interpreted in the sense most favorable to the consumer.

###### Article 1783

The seller has two principal obligations: that of delivering and that of warranting the thing which he sells.

##### Section II : De la délivrance Article 1784

Delivery consists in making available to the purchaser the thing sold so that the latter may use it, enjoy it and dispose of it materially.  
Delivery must take place at the place where, at the time of the sale, the thing which was the subject thereof was located, unless otherwise agreed.

###### Article 1785

The obligation to deliver immovables is fulfilled on the part of the seller when he has handed over the keys, if it is a building, or when he has handed over the title deeds.

###### Article 1786

Delivery of movable effects takes place:	by handing over the thing to the purchaser;	by handing over the keys of the buildings which contain them;  
	or by the mere consent of the parties, if the transport thereof cannot take place at the time of the sale, or if the purchaser already had them in his possession under another title.

###### Article 1787

The delivery of incorporeal rights is effected by the handing over of title deeds, the signing of transfer orders, or by the use that the purchaser makes of them with the consent of the seller.

###### Article 1788

Unless otherwise stipulated, the costs of delivery are borne by the seller, and those of removal are borne by the buyer.

###### Article 1789

If the seller fails to make delivery within the time agreed between the parties, the purchaser may, at his option, demand the rescission of the sale or his being put in possession, if the delay arises only from the act of the seller.  
The burden of proof that he has placed the thing sold at the disposal of the buyer within the agreed time lies with the seller.

###### Article 1790

In all cases where the purchaser suffers damage as a result of failure to deliver at the agreed time, the seller is ordered to pay him compensatory damages.

###### Article 1791

The seller is not bound to deliver the thing if the buyer does not pay the price, and the seller has not granted him a period of time for payment.  
Nor shall he be obliged to deliver, even though he has granted a period of time for payment, if, since the sale, the buyer has become bankrupt, so that the seller is in imminent danger of losing the price; unless the buyer gives him security to pay at the term.

###### Article 1792

The thing must be delivered in the state in which it is at the time of the sale.  

From that day, unless otherwise agreed, all fruits belong to the purchaser.

###### Article 1793

The obligation to deliver the thing includes its accessories and everything that has been intended for its perpetual use.

###### Article 1794

The seller is bound to deliver the area as it is stated in the contract, subject to the modifications hereinafter expressed.

###### Article 1795

If the sale of immovable property has been made with indication of the area, at so much per measure, the seller is obliged to deliver to the purchaser, if he requires it, the quantity indicated in the contract; if this is not possible for him or if the purchaser does not require it, the seller is obliged to suffer a proportional reduction of the price.  
If, on the contrary, the area is greater than that expressed in the contract, the purchaser has the choice of providing the supplement of the price, or of withdrawing from the contract, if the excess is one-twentieth above the declared area.

###### Article 1796

In all other cases of sale of immovable property, which have therefore not been made at so much per measure, the deficiency in area can give rise, in favour of the purchaser, only to a reduction of the price when the difference in less reaches one-twentieth, and, in favour of the seller only to an increase of the price when the difference in more reaches one-twentieth, all subject to stipulation to the contrary.

###### Article 1797

In the case where, according to Article 1796, there is ground for an increase of price for excess of measurement, the purchaser has the choice either of withdrawing from the contract or of providing the supplement of the price, and this, with interest if he has kept the immovable property.

###### Article 1798

In all cases where the purchaser has the right to withdraw from the contract, the seller is bound to restore to him, in addition to the price, if he has received it, the costs of that contract.

###### Article 1799

The action for supplement of price on the part of the seller of the immovable property, and that for reduction of price or for rescission of the contract on the part of the purchaser of that property, must be brought within one year, from the day of the contract, on pain of forfeiture.

###### Article 1800

If two pieces of land have been sold by the same contract, and for one and the same price, with designation of the measurement of each, and there is found to be less area in one and more in the other, compensation is made up to due concurrence; and the action, either for supplement or for reduction of the price, takes place only according to the rules established above.

###### Article 1801

The question of knowing upon which, of the seller or of the purchaser, must fall the loss or deterioration of the thing sold before delivery, is decided according to the rules prescribed in the title Of Obligations.

##### Section III: Of the warranty of the seller Article 1802

The warranty that the seller owes to the purchaser of any right of ownership, corporeal or incorporeal, has two objects:	the first is the peaceful possession of the thing sold;	the second, the hidden defects of that thing or the redhibitory defects.

###### § 1. Of the warranty in case of eviction

###### Article 1803

Even if the sale contains no stipulation on the warranty, the seller is obliged by law to warrant the purchaser against the eviction that he suffers in the whole or part of the object sold, or of the charges claimed on that object, and not declared at the time of the sale.

###### Article 1804

The parties may, by particular agreements, add to this obligation by law, or diminish its effect.  

The parties may even agree that the seller shall be subject to no warranty; in that case, the seller nevertheless remains bound by the warranty that results from an act personal to him. Any agreement to the contrary is null.

###### Article 1805

Even if a clause of non-warranty has been stipulated, the seller, in case of eviction, is nevertheless bound to the restitution of the price, unless the purchaser knew at the time of the sale of the danger of eviction or unless he purchased at his own peril and risk.

###### Article 1806

When the warranty has been promised, or when nothing has been stipulated on that subject, if the purchaser is evicted, he has the right to demand against the seller the reparation of all the prejudice caused by the non-performance of the contract, namely:
1° The restitution of the price;  
2° The restitution of the fruits, when he is obliged to render them to the owner who evicts him;  
3° The costs incurred on the demand for warranty of the buyer, and those incurred by the original claimant; 4° Finally, the damages and interest, as well as the costs and fair costs of the contract.

###### Article 1807

When at the time of eviction, the thing sold is found to be diminished in value, or considerably deteriorated, whether by the negligence of the buyer, or by accidents of force majeure, the seller is nevertheless bound to restore the whole of the price.  
But if the purchaser has derived profit from the degradations made by him, for example, by selling the materials that he has removed from the thing or decorative elements, the seller has the right to retain from the price a sum equal to that profit.  
Conversely, the seller is bound to reimburse or to have reimbursed to the purchaser, by the person who evicts him, all the useful repairs and improvements that he has made to the land.

###### Article 1808

On the other hand, if the thing sold is found to have increased in price at the time of eviction, independently even of the act of the purchaser, the seller is bound to pay him the amount of that increase in value in relation to the price of the sale.

###### Article 1809

If the seller has sold in bad faith the land of another, he is obliged to reimburse to the purchaser all the expenses, even voluptuary or of amenity, that the latter has incurred on the land.

###### Article 1810

If the purchaser is evicted only of a part of the thing but it is so essential that the purchaser would not have purchased without it, he may have the sale rescinded.  
In this case of partial eviction, when the sale is not rescinded, the value of the part of which the purchaser is evicted is reimbursed to him according to the valuation at the time of eviction, and not proportionally to the total price of the sale, regardless of whether the thing sold has increased or diminished in value.

###### Article 1811

If the property that has been sold is found to be encumbered, without any declaration having been made, by non-apparent servitudes, and they are of such importance that there is reason to presume that the purchaser would not have bought had he been informed of them, he may demand, at his choice, rescission of the contract or compensation.

Other questions to which damages may give rise resulting for the purchaser from non-performance of the sale must be decided according to the general rules established in the title On Obligations.

###### Article 1812

The warranty for eviction ceases when the purchaser has allowed himself to be condemned by a final judgment, or from which appeal is no longer admissible, without calling his vendor, if the latter proves that there existed sufficient means to have the claim rejected.

###### § 2. De la garantie des défauts de la chose vendue Article 1813

The seller is bound by the warranty by reason of hidden defects in the thing sold which render it unfit for the use for which it is intended, or which so diminish that use that the buyer would not have acquired it, or would have given only a lesser price, had he known of them.

###### Article 1814

The seller is not bound for apparent defects and of which the buyer could have satisfied himself.

###### Article 1815

The seller of an immovable to be constructed cannot be discharged, either before reception of the works, or before the expiration of a period of one month after taking possession by the purchaser, from defects of construction or defects of conformity then apparent.  
There is no ground for rescission of the contract or reduction of the price if the seller undertakes to repair the defect.

###### Article 1816

The seller is bound for hidden defects, even though he did not know of them, unless, in that case, he has stipulated that he will be bound to no warranty.

###### Article 1817

In the cases of articles 1813 and 1816, the buyer has the choice of returning the thing and having the price restituted to him, or of keeping the thing and having part of the price returned to him, as it shall be fixed by the judge who may, where appropriate, appoint an expert.

###### Article 1818

If the seller knew of the defects of the thing, he is bound, in addition to restitution of the price he received for it, for all damages towards the buyer.  
If the seller was unaware of the defects of the thing, he is bound only to restitution of the price, and to reimburse to the purchaser the costs occasioned by the sale.

###### Article 1819

The seller of an immovable to be constructed is bound, from reception of the works, by the obligations of which architects, contractors and other persons bound to the owner by a contract for work are themselves bound pursuant to articles 1950 and following of this code.  
These warranties benefit successive owners of the immovable.  

There will be no ground for rescission of the sale or reduction of the price if the seller undertakes to repair the damage defined in articles 1953, 1954 and 1955 of this code and to assume the warranty provided for in article 1956.

###### Article 1820

If the thing which had defects has perished as a result of its poor quality, the loss is for the seller, who shall be bound towards the buyer to restitution of the price and to the other compensation explained in articles 1818 and 1819.  
But loss occurring by fortuitous event shall be for the account of the buyer.

###### Article 1821

The action resulting from redhibitory defects must be brought by the purchaser, within a brief period, according to the nature of the redhibitory defects, and the usage of the place where the sale was made.  
In the case provided for by article 1815, the action must be brought, on pain of forfeiture, within the year following the date on which the seller may be discharged from apparent defects.

###### Article 1822

It does not take place in sales made by authority of justice.

#### Chapitre VI. Des obligations de l'acheteur Article 1823

The principal obligation of the buyer is to pay the price on the day and at the place settled by the sale.

###### Article 1824

If nothing has been settled in that regard at the time of the sale, the buyer must pay at the place and at the time when delivery is to be made.

###### Article 1825

The buyer owes interest on the price of the sale until payment of the capital, in the following three cases:	if it was so agreed at the time of the sale;	if the thing sold and delivered produces fruits or other revenues;	if the buyer has been summoned to pay. In this last case, interest runs only from the summons.

###### Article 1826

If the buyer is disturbed or has just cause to fear being disturbed by an action, whether hypothecary or in revendication, he may suspend payment of the price until the seller has caused the disturbance to cease, unless the latter prefers to give security, or unless it has been stipulated that, notwithstanding the disturbance, the buyer shall pay.

###### Article 1827

If the buyer does not pay the price, the seller may demand rescission of the sale.

###### Article 1828

Rescission of the sale of immovables is pronounced immediately, if the seller is in danger of losing the thing and the price.  
If this danger does not exist, the judge may grant to the purchaser a longer or shorter period according to the circumstances.  

This period having passed without the purchaser having paid, rescission of the sale shall be pronounced.

###### Article 1829

If it has been stipulated at the time of the sale of immovables that, for want of payment of the price within the agreed term, the sale would be rescinded by operation of law, the purchaser may nevertheless pay after expiration of the period, as long as he has not been put on notice by a summons; but, after this summons, the judge cannot grant him this period.

###### Article 1830

In matters of sale of commodities and movable effects, rescission of the sale shall take place by operation of law and without summons, for the benefit of the seller, after expiration of the term agreed for withdrawal.

#### Chapitre VII. De la nullité et de la résolution de la vente Article 1831

Independently of the causes of nullity or rescission already explained in this title, and of those which are common to all contracts, the contract of sale may be rescinded by exercise of the right of redemption and by vileness of the price.

##### Section I : De la faculté de rachat Article 1832

The right of redemption is a pact by which the seller reserves to himself the right to take back the thing sold, upon restitution of the principal price and the reimbursement set out in article 1843.

###### Article 1833

The right of redemption cannot be stipulated for a term exceeding five years. The fixed term is strict and cannot be extended by the judge.  
If it has been stipulated for a longer term, it is reduced to this term of five years.

###### Article 1834

For want of the seller having exercised his action of redemption within the prescribed term, the purchaser remains irrevocable owner.  
The period runs against all persons, even against the minor, subject, if there is ground, to recourse against the person to whom this omission is imputable.

###### Article 1835

The seller with a pact of redemption may exercise his action against a second purchaser, even though the right of redemption had not been declared in the second contract.

###### Article 1836

The purchaser with a pact of redemption exercises all the rights of his seller; he may prescribe both against the true owner and against those who would claim rights or hypothecs on the thing sold.

###### Article 1837

He may raise the benefit of discussion against the creditors of his seller.

###### Article 1838

If the purchaser with a pact of redemption of a part of an undivided property has become the successful bidder for the whole on a partition sale provoked against him, he may oblige the seller to redeem the whole when the latter wishes to use the pact.

###### Article 1839

If several persons have jointly sold, by a single contract, property held in common between them, each may exercise the action for redemption only for the share he had in it.  
The same applies if the person who sold property alone has left several heirs. But each of these co-heirs may exercise the right of redemption only for the share he takes in the succession.

###### Article 1840

However, in the case of the preceding article, the purchaser may require that all the co-vendors or all the co-heirs be joined as parties, in order to reach an agreement among themselves for the recovery of the thing sold in its entirety; and, if they do not reach an agreement, the purchaser may retain the thing in its entirety, except that the person who exercised the action for redemption who has not obtained the agreement of the others may exercise the action for the whole and pay the entire price and costs of the sale.

###### Article 1841

If the sale of property belonging to several persons was not made jointly and as a whole, and each has therefore sold only the share he had in it, these persons may separately exercise the action for redemption on the portion that belonged to them.  
The purchaser, in this case, cannot compel the person who exercises the action for his share to redeem the whole.

###### Article 1842

If the purchaser has left several heirs, the action for redemption may be exercised against each of them only for his share, in the case where it is still undivided, and in the case where the thing sold has been divided among them.  
But if there has been a partition of the succession and the thing sold has fallen to the lot of one of the heirs, the action for redemption may be brought against him for the whole.  
The parties may stipulate that in case of death of the purchaser leaving several heirs, the redemption shall be effected, against these heirs, only for the whole. Likewise, several persons acquiring jointly subject to a redemption pact may stipulate that the vendor shall not exercise partial redemption.

###### Article 1843

The vendor who exercises the redemption pact must reimburse not only the principal price, but also the costs and lawful expenses of the sale, the necessary repairs, and those which have increased the value of the property, up to the amount of that increase. He may not enter into possession of the property until he has satisfied all these obligations.  
When the redemption pact has been duly published at the mortgage registry, all charges and mortgages with which the purchaser may have encumbered it subsequent to the sale are unenforceable against the vendor who redeems his property. He is however bound to perform leases made without fraud by the purchaser.

##### Section II: Of the annulment of the sale on grounds of lesion Article 1844

If the vendor has suffered lesion of more than seven-twelfths in the price of immovable property, he has the right to demand the nullity of the sale, even in the case where he had expressly renounced in the contract the right to demand this annulment and had declared that he was giving the surplus value.  

The remedy for lesion does not operate in favour of the purchaser.

###### Article 1845

To determine whether there is lesion of more than seven-twelfths, the immovable property must be valued according to its condition and value at the time of the sale.  
In case of a unilateral promise to sell, the lesion is assessed on the day of completion, that is to say at the time of exercise of the option.

###### Article 1846

The claim is no longer admissible after the expiration of two years, from the day of the sale.  

This period runs against spouses and against absentees, adults under guardianship and minors deriving title from an adult who sold.  
This period also runs and is not suspended during the duration of the time stipulated for the redemption pact.

###### Article 1847

In case of disagreement between the parties on the existence of the lesion, the judge may order an expert appraisal only if the claimant alleges facts sufficiently serious for the lesion to appear possible if not probable. In this case, the judge appoints, ex officio or upon joint and unanimous choice of the parties for each of the experts, a panel of three experts. They must prepare a joint report, in which they shall express a single opinion on the existence or non-existence of the lesion, by majority vote.  
If nevertheless different opinions remain, the report shall contain the reasons therefor, without it being permitted to disclose which opinion each expert held.

###### Article 1848

In the case where the action for nullity is allowed, the purchaser has the choice:
1° to return the thing by withdrawing the price he paid for it;  
2° to keep the property by paying the supplement of the fair price, less one-tenth of the total price. The third-party possessor has the same right, subject to his warranty against his vendor.

###### Article 1849

If the purchaser prefers to keep the thing by providing the supplement determined by the preceding article, he must pay interest on the supplement from the day of the claim for nullity.  
If he prefers to return it and receive the price, he returns the fruits from the day of the claim.  

Interest on the price he paid is also counted to him from the day of the same claim, or from the day of payment, if he has received no fruits.

###### Article 1850

Sales which must be made by judicial authority cannot be the subject of an action for nullity on grounds of lesion.

###### Article 1851

The rules explained in the preceding section for cases where several have sold jointly or separately, and for the case where the vendor or the purchaser has left several heirs, are likewise observed for the exercise of the action for nullity.

#### Chapter VIII. Of licitation

###### Article 1852

Licitation consists in the sale by auction, on a voluntary basis, of movable or immovable property held in indivision, by the holders of real rights over that thing.  
The sale is followed by a distribution of its proceeds by allocation to each co-owner of a portion corresponding to his undivided rights.

###### Article 1853

Each of the co-owners has the right to request that third parties be admitted to participate in the bidding. They are necessarily called when one of the co-owners is a minor.

###### Article 1854

The method and formalities to be observed for licitation are explained in the title On Successions and in the Code of Civil Procedure.

#### Chapter IX. Of the transfer of debts and other incorporeal rights Article 1855

In the transfer of a right or an action against a third party, delivery is effected between the transferor and the transferee by the handing over of the title.

###### Article 1856

The transferee is seized with respect to third parties only by service of notice of the transfer made to the debtor.  

Nevertheless, the transferee may also be seized by acceptance of the transfer made by the debtor in an authentic act.

###### Article 1857

If, before the transferor or the transferee had served notice of the transfer to the debtor, the debtor had paid the transferor, he shall be validly discharged.

###### Article 1858

A person who sells an incorporeal right must warrant its existence at the time of the transfer, even though it is made without warranty.

###### Article 1859

A person who sells a succession without specifying in detail the objects thereof is bound to warrant only his status as heir.  
If he had already enjoyed the fruits of a thing present in that succession, or received the amount of a debt found therein, or sold property nevertheless belonging to the succession, he is bound to reimburse them to the purchaser, unless otherwise stipulated at the time of sale.  

The purchaser must for his part reimburse to the vendor of the succession what the latter has paid for the debts and charges thereof, and any claim that the latter could have against the succession, unless otherwise stipulated.

###### Article 1860

The assignment of litigious rights operates as a transfer of the assignor's right to the assignee by substituting the latter for the former in the pending proceedings.

Nevertheless, the person against whom a litigious right has been assigned may, either by extrajudicial act or by way of principal submissions filed in the pending proceedings, be discharged from it by the assignee, by reimbursing him the actual price of the assignment together with costs and expenses, and with interest from the day on which the assignee paid the price of the assignment made to him.

###### Article 1861

A thing is deemed litigious as soon as there are proceedings and contestation on the merits of the right.

###### Article 1862

The assigned debtor may not benefit from the right of litigious withdrawal:
1° In the case where the assignment has been made to a co-heir or co-owner of the assigned right; 2° When it has been made to a creditor in payment of what is owed to him;
3° When it has been made to the possessor of the property subject to the litigious right.

###### Article 1863

Articles 1855 to 1858 do not apply to assignments governed by Articles 1507 to 1512 of this code.

### Title VIII: Exchange

###### Article 1864

Exchange is a contract by which the parties respectively give each other one thing for another.

###### Article 1865

Exchange is effected by consent alone, in the same manner as sale.

###### Article 1866

If one of the co-exchangers has already received the thing given to him in exchange, and he subsequently proves that the other contracting party is not the owner of that thing, he may not be forced to deliver that which he promised in counter-exchange, but only to return that which he received.

###### Article 1867

The co-exchanger who is evicted from the thing he received in exchange has the choice of claiming damages or compelling the other party to restore his thing to him.

###### Article 1868

Rescission on grounds of lesion does not apply to the contract of exchange.

###### Article 1869

All other rules prescribed for the contract of sale apply to exchange.

### Title IX: The contract of lease

Chapter I. General provisions Article 1870
There are two kinds of lease contracts: that of things, and that of work and industry.

###### Article 1871

The lease of things is a contract by which one of the parties undertakes to give the other the enjoyment of a thing for a certain time, and for a certain price which the latter undertakes to pay him.

The lease contract confers on the lessee only a movable and personal right.
The rules applicable to the lease contract do not apply to the emphyteutic lease, which is subject to its own rules.

###### Article 1872

The lease of work and industry is a contract by which one of the parties undertakes to do something for the other, for a price agreed between them.
Estimates, contracts or fixed prices, for the undertaking of a work for a determined price, are also a lease, when the material is supplied by the person for whom the work is done.

###### Article 1873

Leases of national property, property of communes and public establishments are subject to special regulations.

#### Chapter II. The lease of things Article 1874

All movable and immovable property that is in commerce may be the subject of a lease contract.

##### Section I: Provisions common to leases Article 1875

The lease contract may be made in writing or verbally.
If the lease made without writing has not yet received any performance, and one of the parties denies it, proof may not be received by witnesses, even if the stated price is modest. The possible payment of a sum of money, without further specification, does not constitute commencement of performance of the verbal lease. The oath may only be deferred to the person who denies the lease.

###### Article 1876

When there is a dispute over the price of a verbal lease whose performance has commenced and there is no receipt, the lessee has the choice between two modes of proof to establish the price of the lease: oath or expert assessment. If he opts for the oath, the owner shall be believed on his word; if he opts for expert assessment, the costs thereof shall remain at the lessee's expense if the valuation should exceed the price he declared.
The judge may neither apply the provisions of the preceding paragraph of his own motion nor, when seized of the question, fix the rent on the basis of elements other than those provided for in the text.

###### Article 1877

The lessee has the right to sublet, and even to assign his lease to a third party, if this option has not been prohibited to him, in whole or in part, by the contract.
When the clause prohibiting subletting or assignment of the lease is pure and simple, it applies absolutely and the lessee must respect it, even if he were to demonstrate that the lessor has no interest in requiring its application and that he himself has an important interest in subletting or assigning his lease

###### Article 1878

Article 722, paragraph 4, is applicable to leases of property of minors.

###### Article 1879

The lessor is obliged, by the nature of the contract, and without any need for any special stipulation: 1° To deliver to the lessee the leased thing;
2° To maintain that thing in a condition fit to serve the use for which it was leased;
3° To ensure the lessee peaceful enjoyment of the leased thing throughout the duration of the lease; 4° To ensure, if there are any, the permanence and quality of plantations.

###### Article 1880

The lessor is bound to deliver the thing in good repair of every kind.

He must make thereto, during the duration of the lease, all repairs that may become necessary, other than tenancy repairs. The owner thus bears the cost of major repairs due to age or poor workmanship; he must also guarantee his lessee against all defects or faults of the leased thing that prevent its use, even if the lessor was not aware of them at the time of the lease. If any loss should result to the lessee from these defects or faults, the lessor would be bound to compensate him.

###### Article 1881

The tenant may not claim reimbursement from his owner for major repairs that he would have carried out without the latter's prior agreement.

###### Article 1882

It is otherwise if, during the lease, the leased thing needs urgent repairs that cannot be deferred, when the lessor cannot be contacted or is slow to react: the tenant may then have the works carried out without requesting authorization in advance from his owner; he may subsequently obtain reimbursement.
Conversely, if such repairs are undertaken by the lessor during the lease, the lessee must suffer them, whatever inconvenience they may cause him, and even if he must be deprived, while they are being done, of part of the leased thing.

But, if these repairs last more than thirty days, the price of the lease shall be reduced in proportion to the time and the part of the leased thing of which he has been deprived. And, if the repairs are of such a nature that they render uninhabitable what is necessary for the accommodation of the lessee and his family, the latter may have the lease terminated.

###### Article 1883

The lessor may not, during the duration of the lease, change the form of the leased thing.

###### Article 1884

The lessee is bound by two principal obligations:
1° To use the leased thing as a normally diligent person, and according to the purpose given to it by the lease, or according to that presumed from the circumstances, in the absence of agreement;
2° To pay the rent, price of the lease, at the agreed terms.

###### Article 1885

If the lessee uses the leased thing contrary to the obligations imposed on him, or according to a use from which damage could result to the lessor, the latter may, according to the circumstances, have the lease terminated.

###### Article 1886

If an inventory of fixtures has been made between the lessor and the lessee, the latter must return the thing in the condition in which he received it, according to that inventory.  
If no inventory of fixtures has been made, the lessee is presumed to have received them in good condition of tenantable repairs, and must return them in such condition, unless proof to the contrary is provided.  

In both cases, the lessee is not liable for what has perished or been damaged during the lease, when the harmful event occurred without his fault, for example, due to age, a break-in causing the damage, fortuitous event or fault of the lessor.

###### Article 1887

The lessee must ensure that the premises he occupies are maintained in their condition. He must therefore bear the cost of minor repairs and tenantable repairs, that is to say the routine maintenance of the dwelling and its equipment elements.  
The lessee must bear the cost of major repairs when the damage is due to poor maintenance on his part, excluding age, defective workmanship, construction defect, fortuitous event or force majeure. He is likewise not liable for deterioration related to normal use of the equipment and premises.

###### Article 1888

The lessee is however liable for damage and losses that occur through the act of persons of his household or his sub-tenants.

###### Article 1889

The lessee is also liable for fire, unless he proves that the fire occurred by fortuitous event or force majeure, by construction defect, or that the fire was communicated from a neighboring house.  
If there are several tenants, they are jointly and severally liable for the fire, proportionally to the rental value of the part of the building they occupy, unless they prove either that the fire started in the dwelling of one of them, in which case that one alone is liable for it, or that certain ones succeed in proving that the fire could not have started in their premises, in which case those ones are not liable for it.

###### Article 1890

If the lease was made without writing, the lease ends by notice given by one party to the other, observing a reasonable period.  
If it was made in writing, it ceases by operation of law upon expiration of the fixed term, without it being necessary to give notice.

###### Article 1891

If, upon expiration of written leases, the lessee remains in the premises and is left in possession by the lessor, a new lease is created whose effect is governed by Article 1890 paragraph one relating to leases made without writing.  
In this case, the security given for the lease does not extend to obligations resulting from the extension.

###### Article 1892

The lessor is not required to guarantee the lessee against disturbance that third parties bring by acts of trespass to his enjoyment, without moreover claiming any right over the leased thing; except for the lessee to pursue them in his personal name.  
The perpetrators of an act of trespass cannot justify it on the pretext of a right they might have over the thing. The judge shall order restoration and cessation of the disturbance, and shall invite the interested parties to act according to legal channels.  
If, on the contrary, the tenant has been disturbed in his enjoyment as a result of an action concerning the ownership of the property, he is entitled to a proportionate reduction in the lease price, provided that the disturbance and impediment have been reported to the owner.

###### Article 1893

If the lessee is himself summoned to court by a third party who intends to have him condemned to surrender all or part of that thing, or to suffer the exercise of some servitude, that lessee must call the lessor in warranty, and must be removed from the proceedings, if he so requires, by naming the lessor for whom he possesses.

###### Article 1894

If, during the term of the lease, the leased thing is destroyed or lost in its entirety by fortuitous event, the lease is terminated by operation of law; if it is only partially destroyed, the lessee may, depending on the circumstances, request either a reduction in price, or even termination of the lease. In either case, there is no entitlement to any compensation.

###### Article 1895

The lease contract is terminated by the respective failure of the lessor and the lessee to fulfill their commitments.

###### Article 1896

The lease contract is not terminated by the death of the lessor nor by that of the lessee.

###### Article 1897

If the lessor sells the leased thing, the purchaser cannot evict the lessee who has an authentic lease or whose date is certain, unless he reserved that right in the lease contract.

###### Article 1898

If it was agreed, at the time of the lease, that in case of sale the purchaser may evict the lessee, and no stipulation was made regarding damages, the lessor is required to compensate the lessee:
1° In case of lease of a house, apartment or shop, a sum equal to the rent price, for the time which, according to local custom, is granted between notice and departure.  
2° In the case of rural property, a sum equal to one-third of the lease price for all the time remaining to run.  
The amount of compensation is, in case of dispute, fixed by the judge who may, if necessary, appoint an expert.  
As long as the compensation has not been paid, the lessee may remain in the premises.

###### Article 1899

If the lease is not made by authentic act, or does not have a certain date, the purchaser is not liable for any damages.

###### Article 1900

The purchaser with redemption clause cannot use the power to evict the lessee, until, by the expiration of the period fixed for redemption, he becomes definitive owner, except with the agreement of his seller.

###### Article 1901

The purchaser who wishes to use the power reserved by the lease, to evict the lessee in case of sale is required to give notice to the lessee, for a duration as provided in the lease contract for notices in case of termination and, failing that, for a reasonable duration.

##### Section II: Specific Rules

###### Article 1902

The lease with option to purchase is a lease contract providing that at its term, the tenant may acquire the property at a price fixed in advance.  
When the contract concerns an individual, the transaction is a lease with promise of sale or lease-purchase; when it concerns professionals, it is a finance lease contract governed by the provisions of Law No. 183/AN/17/7th L on finance leases, of May 29, 2017.

###### § 1

Relations between lessors and tenants of residential premises or for professional use without industrial or commercial character

###### Article1903

These provisions are applicable to relations between lessors###### Article 1886

If an inventory of fixtures has been made between the lessor and the lessee, the latter must return the thing in the condition in which he received it, according to that inventory.  
If no inventory of fixtures has been made, the lessee is presumed to have received them in good condition of tenantable repairs, and must return them in such condition, unless proof to the contrary is provided.  

In both cases, the lessee is not liable for what has perished or been damaged during the lease, when the harmful event occurred without his fault, for example, due to age, a break-in causing the damage, fortuitous event or fault of the lessor.

###### Article 1887

The lessee must ensure that the premises he occupies are maintained in their condition. He must therefore bear the cost of minor repairs and tenantable repairs, that is to say the routine maintenance of the dwelling and its equipment elements.  
The lessee must bear the cost of major repairs when the damage is due to poor maintenance on his part, excluding age, defective workmanship, construction defect, fortuitous event or force majeure. He is likewise not liable for deterioration related to normal use of the equipment and premises.

###### Article 1888

The lessee is however liable for damage and losses that occur through the act of persons of his household or his sub-tenants.

###### Article 1889

The lessee is also liable for fire, unless he proves that the fire occurred by fortuitous event or force majeure, by construction defect, or that the fire was communicated from a neighboring house.  
If there are several tenants, they are jointly and severally liable for the fire, proportionally to the rental value of the part of the building they occupy, unless they prove either that the fire started in the dwelling of one of them, in which case that one alone is liable for it, or that certain ones succeed in proving that the fire could not have started in their premises, in which case those ones are not liable for it.

###### Article 1890

If the lease was made without writing, the lease ends by notice given by one of the parties to the other, observing a reasonable period.  
If it was made in writing, it ceases by operation of law at the expiration of the fixed term, without it being necessary to give notice.

###### Article 1891

If, at the expiration of written leases, the lessee remains in the premises and is left in possession by the lessor, a new lease is created whose effect is governed by Article 1890 paragraph one relating to leases made without writing.  
In this case, the security given for the lease does not extend to obligations resulting from the extension.

###### Article 1892

The lessor is not required to guarantee the lessee against disturbance that third parties bring by acts of trespass to his enjoyment, without moreover claiming any right over the leased thing; except for the lessee to pursue them in his personal name.  
The perpetrators of an act of trespass cannot justify it on the pretext of a right they might have over the thing. The judge shall order restoration and cessation of the disturbance, and shall invite the interested parties to act according to legal means.  
If, on the contrary, the tenant has been disturbed in his enjoyment as a result of an action concerning the ownership of the property, he is entitled to a proportionate reduction in the lease price, provided that the disturbance and impediment have been reported to the owner.

###### Article 1893

If the lessee is himself summoned to court by a third party who intends to have him condemned to surrender all or part of that thing, or to suffer the exercise of some servitude, that lessee must call the lessor in warranty, and must be removed from the proceedings, if he so requires, by naming the lessor for whom he possesses.

###### Article 1894

If, during the term of the lease, the leased thing is destroyed or lost in its entirety by fortuitous event, the lease is terminated by operation of law; if it is only partially destroyed, the lessee may, depending on the circumstances, request either a reduction in price, or even termination of the lease. In either case, there is no entitlement to any compensation.

###### Article 1895

The lease contract is terminated by the respective failure of the lessor and the lessee to fulfill their commitments.

###### Article 1896

The lease contract is not terminated by the death of the lessor nor by that of the lessee.

###### Article 1897

If the lessor sells the leased thing, the purchaser cannot evict the lessee who has an authentic lease or whose date is certain, unless he reserved that right in the lease contract.

###### Article 1898

If it was agreed, at the time of the lease, that in case of sale the purchaser may evict the lessee, and no stipulation has been made regarding damages, the lessor is required to compensate the lessee:
1° In case of lease of a house, apartment or shop, a sum equal to the rent price, for the time which, according to local custom, is granted between notice and departure.  
2° In the case of rural property, a sum equal to one third of the lease price for all the time remaining to run.  
The amount of compensation is, in case of dispute, fixed by the judge who may, if necessary, appoint an expert.  
As long as the compensation has not been paid, the lessee may remain in the premises.

###### Article 1899

If the lease is not made by authentic act, or does not have a certain date, the purchaser is not liable for any damages.

###### Article 1900

The purchaser with redemption clause cannot use the power to evict the lessee, until, by the expiration of the period fixed for redemption, he becomes definitive owner, except with the agreement of his seller.

###### Article 1901

The purchaser who wishes to use the power reserved by the lease, to evict the lessee in case of sale is required to give notice to the lessee, for a duration as provided in the lease contract for notices in case of termination and, failing that, for a reasonable duration.

##### Section II: Specific Rules

###### Article 1902

The lease with option to purchase is a lease contract providing that at its term, the tenant may acquire the property at a price fixed in advance.  
When the contract concerns an individual, the transaction is a lease with promise of sale or lease-purchase; when it concerns professionals, it is a finance lease contract governed by the provisions of Law No. 183/AN/17/7th L on finance leases, of May 29, 2017.

###### § 1

Relations between lessors and tenants of residential premises or for professional use without industrial or commercial character

###### Article1903

These provisions are applicable to relations between lessors and tenants or occupants of premises belonging to the following categories:
1° Premises for residential use, with the exception of hotels and boarding houses; 2° Premises for professional use without commercial and industrial character;  
3° Premises leased by a legal person under public law to install services or agents;  
4° Premises leased by legal persons carrying out a non-profit activity, in particular by registered associations and professional unions;  
5° Premises leased by commercial or industrial enterprises for the exclusive residential use of their personnel.  
These provisions do not apply either to relations between legal persons under public law and their agents or to relations between commercial or industrial enterprises and their personnel, with regard to premises allocated to the housing of these agents or this personnel, when housing constitutes a benefit in kind accessory to remuneration within the framework of the regulatory status of civil servants, or the provisions of the labor code for private sector employees.  

A.	Rent

###### Article1904

The amount of rent for leases covered by this section, as well as the conditions for its revision, are freely determined by agreement of the parties upon conclusion of the initial lease between the lessor and the lessee.

###### Article1905

When the lease does not provide for specific conditions for the revision of rent, the latter, unless otherwise stipulated in the lease contract, may be revised at the request of one of the parties when a change in the inflation rate has occurred since the conclusion of the lease or since the last revision of rent, such as to cause this rate to vary by more than ten percent.  
The revision requested may not exceed the justified variation in the inflation rate during the period considered.  

The request for revision must specify the new rent requested or offered and provide all details on the elements taken into consideration to justify the amount of the revision.

###### Article1906

The request for revision of rent made pursuant to article 1905 may not, in any event, be made less than two years after the date of entry into enjoyment by the lessee, or after the starting point of the renewed lease, or after the last revision.

###### Article 1907

In addition to the elements mentioned in article 1905 that may justify a revision, a request for revision may be made by the owner who has made improvements to the substance, comfort or amenity of the leased premises, with the express agreement of the lessee. This agreement must also cover the increase in rental value that will result from these improvements. The new rent thus revised may take effect upon completion of these improvements.  
However, if the owner wishes to make improvements to the premises dictated by hygiene concerns, the prior agreement of the lessee is not necessary. The increase in rental value that will result from these improvements will justify a revision of rent in proportion to the expenses incurred.  

On the other hand, improvements made by the lessee may not be taken into account for a revision of rent.

###### Article1908

In the absence of agreement between the parties on the revision requested pursuant to articles 1905 and 1907 (second paragraph), disputes are brought before the President of the Court of First Instance or before the judge replacing him, who shall rule on the request.

###### Article1909

The lease contract may provide for payment by the lessee, upon entry into the premises, of a security deposit as guarantee for possible damages and settlement of accrued rents. The amount of the security deposit, which may not exceed two months' rent, shall be returned to the lessee upon expiration of the lease, except in case of renewal.

###### Article 1910

In case of sublease, the amount of the sublease price may not exceed the amount of rent owed by the principal lessee to the owner, unless the premises have been furnished or have received improvements by the principal lessee, in which case the rent increase must be in proportion to the expenses incurred.  
The sublessee is liable to the owner only up to the amount of his sublease price of which he may be debtor at the time of seizure, and without being able to invoke payments made in advance.  

Payments made by the sublessee, either by virtue of a stipulation in his lease or as a consequence of the use of the premises, are not deemed to be made in advance.  
In the case of partial sublease, the rent must be at most equal to a fraction of the principal rent proportionate to the size of the subleased premises, subject, as in the preceding paragraph, to furniture provided and improvements made by the principal lessee which will justify increases in proportion to the expenses incurred.

###### Article1911

If the lease, or sublease, concerns premises furnished by the owner, or by the principal lessee, the rent may be increased by a rental price for the furniture in proportion to the price of the latter without this additional price being able to exceed the amount of rent for the unfurnished premises.

###### Article1912

In the case where the lessee or occupant is authorized, either amicably or by court order, to carry out maintenance or repair work normally the responsibility of the owner, he may offset the expenses incurred against future rents. In case of departure from the premises before expiration of the debt, he may pursue the owner for reimbursement of the balance owed.

###### Article1913

Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary, the clause inserted in the lease providing for termination by operation of law for failure to pay rent at the agreed deadlines takes effect only one month after the date of the summons or payment order that has remained unsuccessful.  

The formal notice or order must, on pain of nullity, mention this period.  

The president of the court, petitioned by the lessee within the one-month period referred to above, may by order grant him additional periods for payment of rent within the limit of three months.

###### Article 1914

In case of termination of the lease due to the fault of the lessee, the latter is required to pay the agreed rent during the time necessary for reletting by the owner without this period being able to exceed two months, without prejudice to damages that may have resulted from his fault.  

B.	Maintenance in the premises

###### Article 1915

The right to lease premises, without professional or commercial character, that effectively serves as housing for two spouses, whatever their matrimonial regime and notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary and even if the lease was concluded before the marriage.  
In case of divorce or legal separation, this right may be attributed, in consideration of the social and family interests at stake, by the court hearing the petition for divorce or legal separation, to one of the spouses, subject to rights to compensation or indemnity for the benefit of the other spouse.  

In case of death of one of the spouses, the surviving spouse, co-holder of the lease, has an exclusive right to it unless he or she expressly renounces it.

###### Article1916

1° Occupants in good faith of the premises, unfurnished or furnished, defined in Article 1903, if they have lived there for at least one year, benefit as of right and without the completion of any formality from the right to remain in the leased premises, under the clauses and conditions of the original contract not contrary to the provisions of this resolution, the lease continuing by tacit renewal beyond the term fixed by the contract, except for notice given by one or the other of the parties with three months' notice, by extra-judicial act or by process server;  
2° Notice given by the tenant does not have to be justified;  
3° Notice given by the owner must specify, on pain of nullity, the reason for which it is given and apply Articles 1917, 1918 and 1920, subject to the provisions of Articles 1919 and 1921;  
4° Tenants, sub-tenants, assignees of leases are deemed to be in good faith during the term and after the expiration of their contract, as well as occupants who, living in the premises by virtue of or following a written or verbal lease, a regular sub-lease of a regular assignment of a prior lease, perform their obligations;
